desc:
Every value of nums is a valid index of nums. Start at index 0 and repeatedly move with i = nums[i]. The walk visits some indices once (the tail) and then runs forever around a cycle of indices.

Return [tail, cycle], where tail is the number of distinct indices visited before the first index of the cycle, and cycle is the number of distinct indices in the cycle. Index 0 counts in the tail unless it lies on the cycle itself.

Example: nums = [1, 2, 3, 1] walks 0, 1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3, ... so the tail is {0} and the cycle is {1, 2, 3}; the answer is [1, 3]. For nums = [0] the answer is [0, 1].
hints: Record the step number at which each index is first reached. The first time you hit an index again, you can read both lengths off the step numbers. This uses O(n) memory.
To save the memory, think of two runners: one moves one step at a time, the other two steps at a time. If there is a cycle they must meet inside it.

After they meet: a runner restarted at 0 and a runner left at the meeting point, both moving one step per turn, meet at the first index of the cycle after exactly tail turns. Then walk once around from that index to measure the cycle length.
editorial: The walk is the path of a functional graph from a starting node, so its shape is a tail followed by a cycle. With a first-visit table the solution is immediate: when you reach an index that was first seen at step s, and you are now at step t, the tail has s indices and the cycle has t - s.

Floyd's algorithm does the same in O(1) memory. Phase one: tortoise (1 step) and hare (2 steps) start at nums[0] and nums[nums[0]] and move until they meet. Phase two: reset the tortoise to 0 and move both one step per turn; the number of turns until they meet is the tail length, and they meet at the first cycle index. Phase three: from that index step until you return to it; the number of steps is the cycle length.
The same technique is the standard solution of the "find the duplicate number" problem.
solution:
def tailAndCycle(nums):
    tort = nums[0]
    hare = nums[nums[0]]
    while tort != hare:
        tort = nums[tort]
        hare = nums[nums[hare]]
    tort = 0
    tail = 0
    while tort != hare:
        tort = nums[tort]
        hare = nums[hare]
        tail += 1
    cycle = 1
    hare = nums[tort]
    while hare != tort:
        hare = nums[hare]
        cycle += 1
    return [tail, cycle]
